claim: Zebrafish embryonic tissue explants, prepared prior to germ layer induction and lacking extraembryonic tissues, can specify all germ layers and form a seemingly complete mesendoderm anlage.
source: Here, we show that zebrafish embryonic tissue explants, prepared prior to germ layer induction and lacking extraembryonic tissues, can specify all germ layers and form a seemingly complete mesendoderm anlage.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from in situ hybridization showing expression of markers for all germ layers in explants (Figure 1D-G), and immunofluorescence data showing mesendoderm patterning.

claim: Explant organization requires polarized inheritance of maternal factors from dorsal-marginal regions of the blastoderm.
source: Importantly, explant organization requires polarized inheritance of maternal factors from dorsal-marginal regions of the blastoderm.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that removal of dorsal determinants (DD-removed) or preparation of animal pole explants results in reduced Nodal signaling, mesendoderm induction, and extension (Figure 4D-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Induction of endoderm and head-mesoderm, which require peak Nodal-signaling levels, is highly variable in explants, reminiscent of embryos with reduced Nodal signals from the extraembryonic tissues.
source: Moreover, induction of endoderm and head-mesoderm, which require peak Nodal-signaling levels, is highly variable in explants, reminiscent of embryos with reduced Nodal signals from the extraembryonic tissues.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing variable expression of endoderm (sox32) and head mesoderm (hgg, gsc) markers in explants (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J), and compares this to embryos with reduced YSL-derived Nodal signals (Figure 5, Figure 6).

claim: Zebrafish explants do not undergo bona fide self-organization, but rather display features of genetically encoded self-assembly, where intrinsic genetic programs control the emergence of order.
source: Together, these data suggest that zebrafish explants do not undergo bona fide self-organization, but rather display features of genetically encoded self-assembly, where intrinsic genetic programs control the emergence of order.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that explant organization depends on maternal pre-patterning (Figure 4), and that disrupting this pre-patterning (DD-removed, animal pole explants, reaggregates) impairs coordinated mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: Blastoderm explants initially round up in culture, but eventually become 'pear'-shaped by forming an extension.
source: We found that these blastoderm explants initially rounded up in culture, but eventually became 'pear'-shaped by forming an extension (Figure 1B,C, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images showing the morphological changes of explants over time (Figure 1B), and quantifies circularity (Figure 1C).

claim: The extension in explants begins to form when stage-matched control embryos initiate body axis extension at shield stage.
source: Interestingly, this extension began to form when stage-matched control embryos initiated body axis extension at shield stage (Sepich et al., 2005; Solnica-Krezel and Sepich, 2012), pointing at the possibility that these processes might be related.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on body axis extension in embryos and presents temporal data on explant extension formation.

claim: Blastoderm explants form a large luminal cavity, reminiscent of a blastocoel, which is typically positioned at the opposite end of the explant extension.
source: Contrary to intact embryos, however, blastoderm explants formed a large luminal cavity, reminiscent of a blastocoel (Krens et al., 2017), which was typically positioned at the opposite end of the explant extension (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B, Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field and fluorescence images showing the luminal cavity in explants (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and quantifies its position (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Cells within explants complete their rounds of cleavages and divisions following explant preparation, as evidenced by the similar average diameter of explant and stage-matched embryo cells.
source: Importantly, cells within explants appeared to normally complete their rounds of cleavages and divisions following explant preparation, as evidenced by the similar average diameter of explant and stage-matched embryo cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of cell diameter in explants and embryos at different stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The onset of zygotic genome activation (ZGA), as monitored by the expression of the two zygotic genes tbx16 and chrd, is similar in stage-matched embryos and blastoderm explants.
source: Moreover, we found that the onset of zygotic genome activation (ZGA), as monitored by the expression of the two zygotic genes tbx16 and chrd (Gagnon et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2013), was similar in stage-matched embryos and blastoderm explants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression of tbx16 and chrd in embryos and explants at sphere stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Comparable morphological changes can be observed when blastoderm explants are prepared from earlier (64 and 128 cell-stage) or later (high stage) embryos.
source: Finally, comparable morphological changes could be observed when blastoderm explants were prepared from earlier (64 and 128 cell-stage) or later (high stage) embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D), suggesting that the exact time point of explant preparation during pre-gastrula stages has no decisive influence on explant morphogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images and quantification of explant morphology for explants prepared at different stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D).

claim: Ectoderm (gata2) and neuroectoderm (six3) marker genes are expressed predominantly at the opposite end of the explant extended portion, the region where the cavity is also forming.
source: While ectoderm (gata2) and neuroectoderm (six3) marker genes were expressed predominantly at the opposite end of the explant extended portion, the region where the cavity was also forming (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), all mesendoderm and endoderm marker genes were exclusively found within or adjacent to the extension (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression domains of gata2 and six3 in explants (Figure 1D-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: All mesendoderm and endoderm marker genes are exclusively found within or adjacent to the extension in explants.
source: While ectoderm (gata2) and neuroectoderm (six3) marker genes were expressed predominantly at the opposite end of the explant extended portion, the region where the cavity was also forming (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), all mesendoderm and endoderm marker genes were exclusively found within or adjacent to the extension (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression domains of mesendoderm (hgg, ntl, papc, gsc, flh, tbx6, myoD) and endoderm (sox32) markers in explants (Figure 1D-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Markers of posterior axial mesoderm (ntl and flh) are expressed in the central region of the extension, flanked by paraxial and lateral mesoderm (papc, myoD, tbx6).
source: Specifically, we found that markers of posterior axial mesoderm (ntl and flh) were expressed in the central region of the extension, flanked by paraxial and lateral mesoderm (papc, myoD, tbx6) (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression domains of ntl, flh, papc, myoD, and tbx6 in explants (Figure 1D-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Anterior axial mesendoderm markers (hgg and gsc) are found to be expressed at variable positions along the extended region or directly adjacent to it.
source: In contrast, anterior axial mesendoderm markers (hgg and gsc) were found to be expressed at variable positions along the extended region or directly adjacent to it (Figure 1D–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression domains of hgg and gsc in explants (Figure 1D-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Sporadic endoderm progenitors (sox32) can be found throughout the extension.
source: Finally, sporadic endoderm progenitors (sox32) could be found throughout the extension (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression of sox32 in explants (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: On the explant surface, cells express elevated levels of Keratin 4, a marker of enveloping layer (EVL) cell differentiation.
source: On the explant surface, much like in the intact embryo, we found that cells expressed elevated levels of Keratin 4, a marker of enveloping layer (EVL) cell differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The manuscript presents fluorescence images showing krt4::EGFP-CAAX expression in explants and embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).

claim: Blastoderm explants contain all main germ layer progenitors also found in intact embryos and display a seemingly complete patterning of the mesendoderm anlage.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the blastoderm explants contain all main germ layer progenitors also found in intact embryos and display a seemingly complete patterning of the mesendoderm anlage.
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression of markers for all germ layers and different mesendoderm subtypes in explants (Figure 1D-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Although explants undergo extensive morphogenesis, mesendoderm progenitors do not clearly internalize and, instead, organize into an extension.
source: They also indicate that, although explants undergo extensive morphogenesis, mesendoderm progenitors do not clearly internalize and, instead, organize into an extension (Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse imaging showing mesendoderm progenitors organizing into an extension without clear internalization (Video 3).

claim: The explant phenotype is highly reminiscent of the 'exogastrula' phenotype observed in embryos with defective mesendoderm internalization and, more recently, in mouse gastruloids.
source: This is highly reminiscent of the 'exogastrula' phenotype observed in embryos with defective mesendoderm internalization and, more recently, in mouse gastruloids (Beccari et al., 2018; Branford and Yost, 2002; Turner et al., 2017; van den Brink et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on exogastrula phenotypes and compares the explant morphology to these observations.

claim: All YSL marker genes (slc26a1, slc40a1, mxtx2, gata6, camsap1l1) are either not expressed in explants or show only sporadic expression in small groups of blastoderm cells.
source: We found that all of these genes were either not expressed in explants or showed only sporadic expression in small groups of blastoderm cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression of YSL markers in embryos and explants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).

claim: No clearly recognizable syncytium, a hallmark of the YSL in intact embryos, is detected in explants.
source: Moreover, we failed to detect any clearly recognizable syncytium in explants, a hallmark of the YSL in intact embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents fluorescence images showing no syncytium formation in explants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).

claim: Germ layer specification and mesendoderm patterning in blastoderm explants can occur in the absence of the extraembryonic yolk and YSL.
source: Together, these data strongly support the notion that germ layer specification and mesendoderm patterning in blastoderm explants can occur in the absence of the extraembryonic yolk and YSL.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that explants lack YSL markers and syncytium (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), yet still specify all germ layers and pattern mesendoderm (Figure 1D-G).

claim: Both Nodal ligands sqt and cyc are expressed in blastoderm explants.
source: We observed expression of both Nodal ligands sqt and cyc in blastoderm explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), consistent with previous observations in intact embryos (Erter et al., 1998; Fan et al., 2007; Feldman et al., 1998; Rebagliati et al., 1998; van Boxtel et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing expression of sqt and cyc in explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Nuclear localization of phosphorylated SMAD2/3 (pSMAD2/3), a well-established readout of Nodal/TGFβ signaling activation, is detected in cells located close to the wounding site of explants.
source: In addition to this, we detected nuclear localization of phosphorylated SMAD2/3 (pSMAD2/3), a well-established readout of Nodal/TGFβ signaling activation (Economou and Hill, 2020; Schier, 2009; van Boxtel et al., 2015; van Boxtel et al., 2018), in cells located close to the wounding site of explants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), indicative of local Nodal signaling activation.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing pSMAD2/3 nuclear localization in explants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: Blastoderm explants show initially fewer and less bright pSMAD2/3 positive nuclei than intact embryos, but both parameters continue to increase in explants until stage-matched embryos reach shield stage.
source: A comparison of the spatiotemporal dynamics of Nodal signaling establishment between explants and intact embryos further revealed that, while blastoderm explants showed initially fewer and less bright pSMAD2/3 positive nuclei than intact embryos, both parameters continued to increase in explants until stage-matched embryos had reached shield stage (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–J).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data and quantification of pSMAD2/3 positive nuclei in explants and embryos over time (Figure 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-J).

claim: The temporal dynamics of Nodal signaling in intact embryos differs from explants, with nuclear accumulation of pSMAD2/3 peaking by 50% epiboly in embryos.
source: This differs from the temporal dynamics of Nodal signaling in intact embryos, where nuclear accumulation of pSMAD2/3 peaks already by 50% epiboly (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–J).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data and quantification of pSMAD2/3 positive nuclei in embryos over time (Figure 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-J).

claim: The wounding site of blastoderm explants, where Nodal signaling is activated, corresponds to the former blastoderm margin where explants were removed from the yolk cell.
source: Notably, the wounding site of blastoderm explants, where Nodal signaling was activated corresponds to the former blastoderm margin where explants were removed from the yolk cell (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing pSMAD2/3 localization near the wounding site (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-J), and quantifies the distance of pSMAD2/3 positive nuclei from the wounding site (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-J).

claim: Nodal signaling is active in similar cells in embryos and explants.
source: Given that Nodal signaling in intact embryos is initiated in the blastoderm margin (Dubrulle et al., 2015; Harvey and Smith, 2009; Schier, 2009; van Boxtel et al., 2015), this points at the intriguing possibility that Nodal signaling is active in similar cells in embryos and explants.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on Nodal signaling initiation in the blastoderm margin and presents data showing Nodal signaling near the wounding site (former blastoderm margin) in explants (Figure 2A,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-J).

claim: Cells close to the wounding site in explants display only very limited dispersal during explant maturation.
source: This notion was further substantiated by our observation that cells close to the wounding site in explants display only very limited dispersal during explant maturation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse imaging and quantification of cell dispersal in explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-D).

claim: A gradient of BMP signaling is detectable in blastoderm explants, similar to intact embryos.
source: Moreover, similar to intact embryos, a gradient of BMP signaling was also detectable in blastoderm explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F), suggesting that explants might also use a BMP signaling gradient for patterning along their dorsoventral axis.
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data showing BMP signaling components in explants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F).

claim: Blastoderm explants obtained from MZoep mutants fail to extend, indicative of strongly reduced mesendoderm formation.
source: We found that blastoderm explants obtained from MZoep mutants failed to extend, indicative of strongly reduced mesendoderm formation (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images and quantification of explant morphology for MZoep mutant explants (Figure 2E-G).

claim: Proper Nodal signaling is critical for mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis in blastoderm explants, similar to the situation in intact embryos.
source: This suggests that, similar to the situation in intact embryos, proper Nodal signaling is critical for mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis in blastoderm explants.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that MZoep mutant explants fail to extend (Figure 2E-G), and cites previous studies on the role of Nodal signaling in embryos.

claim: Blocking Nodal signaling from 256 cell to shield stage is sufficient to completely abolish mesendoderm induction and explant extension.
source: We found that blocking Nodal signaling from 256 cell to shield stage was sufficient to completely abolish mesendoderm induction and explant extension (Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D), while blocking Nodal signaling after shield stage had no strong impact on these processes (Figure 2E–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images, fluorescence images, and quantification of explant morphology and mesendoderm marker expression for explants treated with Nodal inhibitor at different time periods (Figure 2E-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-D).

claim: Blocking Nodal signaling after shield stage has no strong impact on mesendoderm induction and explant extension.
source: We found that blocking Nodal signaling from 256 cell to shield stage was sufficient to completely abolish mesendoderm induction and explant extension (Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D), while blocking Nodal signaling after shield stage had no strong impact on these processes (Figure 2E–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images, fluorescence images, and quantification of explant morphology and mesendoderm marker expression for explants treated with Nodal inhibitor at different time periods (Figure 2E-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-D).

claim: Nodal signaling functions similarly in embryos and blastoderm explants, with an early requirement for mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis.
source: This is highly reminiscent of the early requirement of Nodal signaling for mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis in intact embryos (Gritsman et al., 1999; Hagos and Dougan, 2007; Pinheiro and Heisenberg, 2020), suggesting that Nodal signaling functions similarly in embryos and blastoderm explants.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the temporal requirement of Nodal signaling in explants (Figure 2E-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-D), and cites previous studies on the role of Nodal signaling in embryos.

claim: Blastoderm explants prepared from MZ mutants for the Wnt/PCP components wnt11, wnt5b and fz7a/b exhibit reduced or no extension.
source: Blastoderm explants prepared from MZ mutants for the Wnt/PCP components wnt11, wnt5b and fz7a/b also exhibited reduced or no extension (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images and quantification of explant morphology for MZwnt11, MZwnt5b, and MZfz7a/b mutant explants (Figure 3A-D).

claim: Explant extension, similar to body axis elongation in intact embryos, critically depends on non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling.
source: This suggests that explant extension, similar to body axis elongation in intact embryos, critically depends on non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that Wnt/PCP mutant explants have reduced extension (Figure 3A-D), and cites previous studies on the role of Wnt/PCP signaling in body axis elongation.

claim: During explant maturation, the extension length increases, and the width of the non-extended portion decreases.
source: In line with this, we also found that during explant maturation, the extension length increased, and the width of the non-extended portion decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), and that explant extension was largely independent of cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of explant area, width, and extension length over time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C).

claim: Explant extension is largely independent of cell proliferation.
source: In line with this, we also found that during explant maturation, the extension length increased, and the width of the non-extended portion decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), and that explant extension was largely independent of cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images and quantification of explant morphology for explants treated with cell division inhibitors (HUA) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F).

claim: Explants, like intact embryos, might undergo some type of convergence and extension movements, independent of cell proliferation.
source: This points at the intriguing possibility that explants, like intact embryos, might undergo some type of convergence and extension movements, independent of cell proliferation.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that explant extension is independent of cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F), and that extension length increases while width decreases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C).

claim: Elevated levels of nuclear β-cat are detected in blastoderm cells close to the wounding site shortly after explant preparation.
source: Indeed, analysis of nuclear localization of β-cat in explants shortly after preparation revealed elevated levels of nuclear β-cat in blastoderm cells close to the wounding site (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing nuclear β-catenin localization in explants (Figure 4A-C).

claim: In explants, similar to intact embryos, β-cat nuclear accumulation might be responsible for Nodal signaling activation, and consequently, mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis.
source: This suggests that in explants, similar to intact embryos, β-cat nuclear accumulation might be responsible for Nodal signaling activation, and consequently, mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing nuclear β-catenin accumulation near the wounding site (Figure 4A-C), and cites previous studies on the role of β-catenin in Nodal signaling activation in embryos.

claim: In blastoderm explants prepared from DD-removed embryos, nuclear accumulation of β-cat is strongly diminished.
source: As expected, in blastoderm explants prepared from DD-removed embryos, a large portion (>50%) of which displayed a fully ventralized phenotype one day after fertilization (1 dpf), nuclear accumulation of β-cat was strongly diminished (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing reduced nuclear β-catenin in DD-removed explants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: Explants originating from DD-removed embryos show a clear reduction in Nodal signaling and reduced expression of the pan-mesendodermal marker sebox.
source: Interestingly, we found that explants originating from DD-removed embryos showed a clear reduction in Nodal signaling (Figure 4D,E, Video 4) and reduced expression of the pan-mesendodermal marker sebox (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing reduced pSMAD2/3 in DD-removed explants (Figure 4D,E, Video 4), and fluorescence images showing reduced sebox::EGFP expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G).

claim: The proportion of blastoderm explants forming an extension and the degree of explant extension are reduced in DD-removed explants.
source: Consistent with the notion that Nodal-mediated mesendoderm specification was reduced in DD-removed explants, we also found that the proportion of blastoderm explants forming an extension and the degree of explant extension were reduced (Figure 4F–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images and quantification of explant morphology for DD-removed explants (Figure 4F-I).

claim: The extent of mesendoderm induction in DD-removed explants closely correlates with the degree of explant extension at bud stage.
source: Moreover, the extent of mesendoderm induction in DD-removed explants closely correlated with the degree of explant extension at bud stage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript presents a scatter plot showing the correlation between sebox::EGFP domain area and normalized extension length in DD-removed explants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).

claim: In blastoderm explants, maternal deposition of dorsal determinants in cells close to the future wounding site is required for Nodal signaling activation and mesendoderm induction, much more than in embryos that retain Nodal signals emanating from the YSL.
source: This suggests that in blastoderm explants, maternal deposition of dorsal determinants in cells close to the future wounding site is required for Nodal signaling activation and mesendoderm induction, much more than in embryos that retain Nodal signals emanating from the YSL (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing reduced Nodal signaling and mesendoderm induction in DD-removed explants (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H), and compares this to DD-removed embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-F).

claim: CA-Alk8-overexpressing blastoderm explants do not display a strong reduction in the establishment of a Nodal signaling domain.
source: CA-Alk8-overexpressing blastoderm explants did not display a strong reduction in the establishment of a Nodal signaling domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G,H), supporting the notion that β-cat does not affect Nodal signaling through its effect on dorsoventral embryo patterning.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing pSMAD2/3 in CA-Alk8-overexpressing explants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G,H).

claim: AP-derived explants show strongly reduced nuclear pSMAD2/3 accumulation, mesendoderm induction and tissue extension.
source: Moreover, AP-derived explants showed strongly reduced nuclear pSMAD2/3 accumulation, mesendoderm induction and tissue extension (Figure 4D–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–H, Video 4).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing reduced pSMAD2/3 in AP explants (Figure 4D,E, Video 4), fluorescence images showing reduced sebox::EGFP expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H), and bright-field images and quantification of explant morphology (Figure 4F-H).

claim: Maternal pre-patterning by dorsal determinants is needed for proper mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis in blastoderm explants.
source: These findings therefore suggest that maternal pre-patterning by dorsal determinants is needed for proper mesendoderm induction and morphogenesis in blastoderm explants.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that DD-removed and AP explants have reduced Nodal signaling, mesendoderm induction, and extension (Figure 4D-H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H, Video 4).

claim: Blastomere reaggregates undergo progressive compaction and eventually round up in culture.
source: We found that blastomere reaggregates underwent progressive compaction and eventually rounded up in culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse imaging showing blastomere reaggregate compaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).

claim: Reaggregated cells are still capable of undergoing cell divisions, as evidenced by their progressive reduction in cell diameter.
source: Importantly, reaggregated cells were still capable of undergoing cell divisions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), as evidenced by their progressive reduction in cell diameter (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that blastomere reaggregates are viable under culture conditions.
evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse imaging showing cell divisions in reaggregates (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), and quantification of cell diameter over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).

claim: Blastomere reaggregates fail to form a clearly recognizable extension when cultured until stage-matched embryos reach bud stage.
source: Interestingly, we found that even when cultured until stage-matched embryos had reached bud stage, blastomere reaggregates failed to form a clearly recognizable extension (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images and quantification of reaggregate morphology (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D,E).

claim: Expression of the mesodermal marker ntl is restricted to a few sparse cells or seemingly randomly scattered cells within the reaggregates.
source: Consistent with this, we found that expression of the mesodermal marker ntl (Schulte-Merker, 1995; Schulte-Merker et al., 1994) was restricted to a few sparse cells or seemingly randomly scattered cells within the reaggregates (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F–H).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing ntl expression in reaggregates (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F-H).

claim: Neither increasing the cell number within reaggregates nor changing the culture media conditions substantially impacts on reaggregate morphogenesis or its ability to undergo coordinated mesoderm specification.
source: Importantly, neither increasing the cell number within reaggregates nor changing the culture media conditions substantially impacted on reaggregate morphogenesis or its ability to undergo coordinated mesoderm specification (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–H).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images, in situ hybridization data, and quantification of reaggregate morphology and ntl expression for reaggregates prepared at different densities and cultured in different media (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-H).

claim: Maternal pre-patterning and positional information within the blastoderm and, subsequently wounding site of blastoderm explants, is required for coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that maternal pre-patterning and positional information within the blastoderm and, subsequently wounding site of blastoderm explants, is required for coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that reaggregates, which lack positional information, fail to undergo coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-H).

claim: Injection of high amounts of both sqt (2 ng/embryo) and cyc (4 ng/embryo) MOs into the YSL impairs induction of endoderm (sox32) and head mesoderm (hgg and gsc).
source: Consistent with previous observations (Fan et al., 2007), we found that injection of high amounts of both sqt (2 ng/embryo) and cyc (4 ng/embryo) MOs impaired induction of endoderm (sox32) and head mesoderm (hgg and gsc) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), the two mesendoderm progenitor cell types whose induction is thought to require the highest dose of Nodal signaling (Dougan et al., 2003; Gritsman et al., 2000; Schier et al., 1997; Thisse and Thisse, 1999).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing reduced expression of sox32, hgg, and gsc in sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: The induction of notochord (ntl), paraxial (papc) and ventrolateral mesoderm (myoD and tbx6) appears normal in sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos.
source: The induction of notochord (ntl), paraxial (papc) and ventrolateral mesoderm (myoD and tbx6), in contrast, appeared normal in the morphant embryos (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing normal expression of ntl, papc, myoD, and tbx6 in sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Most sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos display severe cyclopia by 32 hpf, indicative of defective induction of anterior mesendoderm structures, but largely normal trunk and tail structures.
source: This also became apparent by 32 hpf, when most morphant embryos displayed severe cyclopia, indicative of defective induction of anterior mesendoderm structures, but largely normal trunk and tail structures (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images showing cyclopia in sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos at 32 hpf (Figure 5B).

claim: The YSL is needed for robust induction of endoderm and head mesoderm, and this signaling source might be specifically required to achieve peak levels of Nodal signaling along the blastoderm margin.
source: Together, these observations suggest that - consistent with previous findings (Fan et al., 2007) - the YSL is needed for robust induction of endoderm and head mesoderm, and that this signaling source might be specifically required to achieve peak levels of Nodal signaling along the blastoderm margin.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing reduced endoderm and head mesoderm induction in sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), and cites previous studies.

claim: YSL-derived Nodal signals are needed to enhance Nodal signaling in the overlying blastoderm.
source: We found a strong and persistent reduction of both the number and intensity of nuclear pSMAD2/3 positive cells along the blastoderm margin in sqt/cyc morphants (Figure 5C–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that YSL-derived Nodal signals are needed to enhance Nodal signaling in the overlying blastoderm.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data and quantification of pSMAD2/3 in sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos (Figure 5C-G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: YSL-specific injection of lower amounts of sqt (1 or 0.4 ng/embryo) and cyc (2 or 0.8 ng/embryo) MOs leads to a dose-dependent reduction in both the number of morphant embryos expressing the ppl marker hgg and the size of the ppl.
source: YSL-specific injection of lower amounts of sqt (1 or 0.4 ng/embryo) and cyc (2 or 0.8 ng/embryo) MOs led to a dose-dependent reduction in both the number of morphant embryos expressing the ppl marker hgg and the size of the ppl, as determined by the expression area of hgg, in those embryos at bud stage (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data and quantification of hgg expression in embryos YSL-injected with different amounts of sqt/cyc MOs (Figure 6A-C).

claim: By 32 hpf, the severity of the cyclopia phenotype closely correlates with the amount of sqt/cyc MOs injected within the YSL.
source: Likewise, by 32 hpf, the severity of the cyclopia phenotype closely correlated with the amount of sqt/cyc MOs injected within the YSL (Figure 5B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents bright-field images showing cyclopia phenotypes in embryos YSL-injected with different amounts of sqt/cyc MOs at 32 hpf (Figure 5B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Endoderm induction, visualized by sox32 expression, is strongly reduced in morphant embryos even with the lowest amount of YSL-injected sqt/cyc MOs (0.4 ng sqt + 0.8 ng cyc MO).
source: Endoderm induction, visualized by sox32 expression (Kikuchi et al., 2001), was also strongly reduced in morphant embryos even with the lowest amount of YSL-injected sqt/cyc MOs (0.4 ng sqt + 0.8 ng cyc MO; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing reduced sox32 expression in embryos YSL-injected with low amounts of sqt/cyc MOs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).

claim: Nodal signaling, assayed by pSMAD2/3 nuclear localization, is decreased to a lesser extent in embryos YSL-injected with low compared to high amounts of sqt/cyc MOs.
source: Consistent with such dose-dependent reduction in head mesoderm and endoderm specification, we found that Nodal signaling, assayed by pSMAD2/3 nuclear localization, was decreased to a lesser extent in embryos YSL-injected with low compared to high amounts of sqt/cyc MOs (2 ng sqt and 4 ng cyc MO) (Figure 6D–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D; compare to Figure 5C–G).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data and quantification of pSMAD2/3 in embryos YSL-injected with different amounts of sqt/cyc MOs (Figure 6D-G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, Figure 5C-G).

claim: Robust induction of head mesoderm and endoderm structures in intact embryos critically relies on the right dosage of extraembryonic Nodal ligands.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that robust induction of head mesoderm and endoderm structures in intact embryos critically relies on the right dosage of extraembryonic Nodal ligands.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing dose-dependent reduction in head mesoderm and endoderm induction with varying amounts of sqt/cyc MOs injected into the YSL (Figure 6A-G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: In explants the induction of head mesoderm and endoderm is highly variable.
source: Notably, we found that in explants the induction of head mesoderm and endoderm was highly variable (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H), and both the size of the ppl and the number of sox32-positive endoderm cells were strongly reduced (Figure 6C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J).
evidence: The manuscript presents in situ hybridization data showing variable expression of hgg and sox32 in explants (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J), and quantification of ppl area (Figure 6C).

claim: Both the size of the ppl and the number of sox32-positive endoderm cells are strongly reduced in explants compared to intact embryos.
source: Notably, we found that in explants the induction of head mesoderm and endoderm was highly variable (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H), and both the size of the ppl and the number of sox32-positive endoderm cells were strongly reduced (Figure 6C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantification of ppl area in explants and embryos (Figure 6C), and in situ hybridization data showing sox32 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J).

claim: The variable induction of head mesoderm and endoderm in explants is consistent with observations from embryo analysis that Nodal signals from the extraembryonic YSL are needed for robust induction of these structures.
source: This is consistent with our observations from the embryo analysis that Nodal signals from the extraembryonic YSL are needed for robust induction of these structures.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing variable head mesoderm and endoderm induction in explants (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J, Figure 6C), and compares this to embryos with reduced YSL-derived Nodal signals (Figure 5, Figure 6).

claim: Maternal factors, initially deposited at the vegetal pole of the oocyte, are required to activate β-cat at the future dorsal side of the embryo and, consequently, initiate Nodal signaling therein.
source: Previous studies have provided evidence that maternal factors, initially deposited at the vegetal pole of the oocyte, are required to activate β-cat at the future dorsal side of the embryo and, consequently, initiate Nodal signaling therein (Langdon and Mullins, 2011; Marlow, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the role of maternal factors in β-catenin activation and Nodal signaling initiation.

claim: Maternal activation of Nodal signaling at the dorsal germ ring margin is required for proper mesoderm induction in blastoderm explants.
source: Our data support this view and show that this maternal activation of Nodal signaling at the dorsal germ ring margin is required for proper mesoderm induction in blastoderm explants.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that DD-removed and AP explants have reduced Nodal signaling and mesendoderm induction (Figure 4D-H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H, Video 4).

claim: Removing dorsal and marginal pre-patterning in AP blastoderm explants or interfering with the spatial distribution of these pre-patterning cues in reaggregates is sufficient to suppress coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis.
source: In particular, our findings that removing dorsal and marginal pre-patterning in AP blastoderm explants or interfering with the spatial distribution of these pre-patterning cues in reaggregates is sufficient to suppress coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis, clearly shows that maternal pre-patterning is indispensable for blastoderm explant organization and morphogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that AP explants and reaggregates have reduced or absent coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis (Figure 4D-H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-H, Video 4).

claim: Maternal pre-patterning is indispensable for blastoderm explant organization and morphogenesis.
source: In particular, our findings that removing dorsal and marginal pre-patterning in AP blastoderm explants or interfering with the spatial distribution of these pre-patterning cues in reaggregates is sufficient to suppress coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis, clearly shows that maternal pre-patterning is indispensable for blastoderm explant organization and morphogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that AP explants and reaggregates have reduced or absent coordinated mesoderm induction and morphogenesis (Figure 4D-H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D-H, Video 4).

claim: The difference in self-organizing capacity between zebrafish explants and ES cell colonies is possibly due to blastoderm cells displaying reduced stemness when compared to ES cells.
source: Possibly, this difference in self-organizing capacity is due to blastoderm cells displaying reduced stemness when compared to ES cells, a plausible assumption given that blastoderm explants were taken from intact embryos that already underwent some degree of embryo polarization and cell fate restriction (Langdon and Mullins, 2011; Marlow, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on embryo polarization and cell fate restriction, and speculates on the difference in stemness between blastoderm cells and ES cells.

claim: Blastoderm explants were cultured in media without serum or other growth factors in order to monitor blastoderm maturation in the absence of any extrinsic signals.
source: Furthermore, we cultured our blastoderm explants in media without serum or other growth factors in order to monitor blastoderm maturation in the absence of any extrinsic signals.
evidence: The manuscript describes the culture conditions used for blastoderm explants.

claim: Stem cell colonies or zebrafish explants were cultured in media supplemented with growth factors and/or serum, which might be required for self-organization to emerge in vitro.
source: In contrast, stem cell colonies or, most recently, also zebrafish explants were cultured in media supplemented with growth factors and/or serum, which might be required for self-organization to emerge in vitro (Baillie-Johnson et al., 2015; Beccari et al., 2018; ten Berge et al., 2008; Turner et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2014; Trivedi et al., 2019; van den Brink et al., 2014; Warmflash et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on stem cell colony and zebrafish explant culture conditions.

claim: Mesendoderm patterning defects in embryos with reduced Nodal signals from the YSL are generally more pronounced than in blastoderm explants.
source: Yet, mesendoderm patterning defects in embryos with reduced Nodal signals from the YSL are generally more pronounced than in blastoderm explants, suggesting that the YSL is more important for robust induction of head mesoderm and endoderm in the intact embryo compared to explants.
evidence: The manuscript presents data comparing mesendoderm patterning in sqt/cyc MO YSL-injected embryos and explants (Figure 5, Figure 6, Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H,J).

claim: One possibility for the embryo-specific requirement of the YSL might be to induce sufficiently high doses of Nodal signaling along the entire blastoderm margin, a requirement less important in explants where the blastoderm margin has collapsed into a single region surrounding the wounding site.
source: One possibility for such embryo-specific requirement of the YSL might be to induce sufficiently high doses of Nodal signaling along the entire blastoderm margin, a requirement less important in explants where the blastoderm margin has collapsed into a single region surrounding the wounding site.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the reason for the embryo-specific requirement of the YSL based on the data presented.

claim: Mesendoderm progenitors do not undergo internalization in explants, but instead form an 'exogastrula'.
source: While blastoderm explants were able to recapitulate a remarkable degree of embryo patterning and morphogenesis, there are still several differences between explants and embryos: foremost, mesendoderm progenitors do not undergo internalization in explants, but instead form an 'exogastrula', similar to previous observations in mouse gastruloids (Baillie-Johnson et al., 2015; Beccari et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2014; van den Brink et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that mesendoderm progenitors organize into an extension without clear internalization (Video 3), and cites previous studies on exogastrula phenotypes.

claim: One possible explanation for the lack of mesendoderm internalization in explants could be that the specific geometry of the embryo is critical for mesendoderm internalization.
source: One possible explanation for this could be that the specific geometry of the embryo is critical for mesendoderm internalization.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the reason for the lack of mesendoderm internalization in explants.

claim: Extraembryonic structures might form a permissive substrate for mesendoderm internalization.
source: Alternatively, extraembryonic structures might form a permissive substrate for mesendoderm internalization.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the role of extraembryonic structures in mesendoderm internalization.

claim: While mesendoderm progenitors fail to internalize in explants, they still form an extension, which - similar to body axis elongation in embryos - depends on Wnt/PCP-signaling.
source: Notably, while mesendoderm progenitors fail to internalize in explants, they still form an extension, which - similar to body axis elongation in embryos - depends on Wnt/PCP-signaling (Čapek et al., 2019; Gray et al., 2011; Solnica-Krezel and Sepich, 2012; Tada and Heisenberg, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that Wnt/PCP mutant explants have reduced extension (Figure 3A-D), and cites previous studies on the role of Wnt/PCP signaling in body axis elongation.

claim: The cellular rearrangements underlying body axis extension in explants and body axis elongation in embryos might be conserved.
source: This suggests that the cellular rearrangements underlying body axis extension in explants and body axis elongation in embryos might be conserved.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that explant extension depends on Wnt/PCP signaling (Figure 3A-D), similar to body axis elongation in embryos.

claim: Cell proliferation does not seem to play a major role in body axis extension in explants or body axis elongation in embryos.
source: Moreover, our and previous observations support that cell proliferation does not seem to play a major role in either of these processes (Liu et al., 2017; Quesada-Hernández et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that explant extension is independent of cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F), and cites previous studies.

claim: Volumetric growth by cell proliferation might function in later stages of explant maturation, similar to its role in tail extension in chick and mouse embryos.
source: Yet, whether volumetric growth by cell proliferation might function in later stages of explant maturation, similar to its role, for instance, in tail extension in chick and mouse embryos (Mongera et al., 2019), remains to be determined.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the role of cell proliferation in tail extension and speculates on its potential role in later stages of explant maturation.

claim: Zebrafish blastoderm explants undergo 'genetically encoded self-assembly', where heterogeneities among cells endowed with a similar genetically encoded cell or developmental program drive the organization of those cells, via local interactions, into the structures they were initially primed to form.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that zebrafish blastoderm explants undergo what has been recently termed 'genetically encoded self-assembly', where heterogeneities among cells endowed with a similar genetically encoded cell or developmental program drive the organization of those cells, via local interactions, into the structures they were initially primed to form (Turner et al., 2016; Xavier da Silveira Dos Santos and Liberali, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that explant organization depends on maternal pre-patterning (Figure 4), and cites previous studies on genetically encoded self-assembly.

claim: Both intrinsic heterogeneities (e.g. maternal factors) and extraembryonic signals might not only be required to render embryonic development predictable and robust, but also to drive the emergence of embryo organization.
source: This interpretation implies that both intrinsic heterogeneities (e.g. maternal factors) and extraembryonic signals might not only be required to render embryonic development predictable and robust, but also to drive the emergence of embryo organization.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the roles of maternal factors and extraembryonic signals in explant organization (Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 6).

claim: Future work will have to address to what extent stem cell colonies/organoids indeed undergo bona fide self-organization, and whether some of their organization might in fact be due to genetically encoded self-assembly.
source: Future work will have to address to what extent stem cell colonies/organoids indeed undergo bona fide self-organization, and whether some of their organization might in fact be due to genetically encoded self-assembly.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on future research directions based on the findings presented.

claim: Amphibians critically rely on maternal factors for precise spatiotemporal activation of morphogen signaling during early embryonic development.
source: While amphibians critically rely on maternal factors for precise spatiotemporal activation of morphogen signaling during early embryonic development, mammalian embryos mostly depend on reciprocal interactions between embryonic and extraembryonic tissues (Mummery and Chuva de Sousa Lopes SM, 2013; Heasman, 2006; Langdon and Mullins, 2011; Stern and Downs, 2012; Tam and Loebel, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the role of maternal factors in amphibian development.

claim: Mammalian embryos mostly depend on reciprocal interactions between embryonic and extraembryonic tissues.
source: While amphibians critically rely on maternal factors for precise spatiotemporal activation of morphogen signaling during early embryonic development, mammalian embryos mostly depend on reciprocal interactions between embryonic and extraembryonic tissues (Mummery and Chuva de Sousa Lopes SM, 2013; Heasman, 2006; Langdon and Mullins, 2011; Stern and Downs, 2012; Tam and Loebel, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the role of embryonic-extraembryonic interactions in mammalian development.

claim: Zebrafish embryos combine features characteristic of both amphibian and mammalian development.
source: Interestingly, zebrafish embryos combine features characteristic of both amphibian and mammalian development.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a known fact about zebrafish development.

claim: In zebrafish, maternal factors initially deposited within the oocyte and signals from extraembryonic tissues, namely the yolk cell and its yolk syncytial layer (YSL), play important roles in germ layer induction and patterning.
source: Here, maternal factors initially deposited within the oocyte (Langdon and Mullins, 2011; Marlow, 2020) and signals from extraembryonic tissues, namely the yolk cell and its yolk syncytial layer (YSL), play important roles in germ layer induction and patterning (Carvalho and Heisenberg, 2010; Chen and Kimelman, 2000; Erter et al., 1998; Fan et al., 2007; Gagnon et al., 2018; Hong et al., 2011; Mizuno et al., 1999; Mizuno et al., 1996; Ober and Schulte-Merker, 1999; Schier and Talbot, 2005; van Boxtel et al., 2015; Veil et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites numerous previous studies on the roles of maternal factors and YSL signals in zebrafish development.

claim: Nodal/TGFβ ligands are initially expressed under maternal control and then secreted by the extraembryonic YSL to pattern the embryonic blastoderm.
source: Nodal/TGFβ ligands, for instance, key signals involved in mesoderm and endoderm (mesendoderm) specification and patterning, are initially expressed under maternal control and then secreted by the extraembryonic YSL to pattern the embryonic blastoderm (Chen and Schier, 2002; Dougan et al., 2003; Erter et al., 1998; Fan et al., 2007; Fauny et al., 2009; Feldman et al., 1998; Gagnon et al., 2018; Gore et al., 2005; Gritsman et al., 2000; Gritsman et al., 1999; Hong et al., 2011; Rebagliati et al., 1998; Rogers et al., 2017; Rogers and Müller, 2019; Thisse and Thisse, 2015; van Boxtel et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites numerous previous studies on Nodal/TGFβ ligand expression and function in zebrafish development.

claim: Human and mouse embryonic stem cell (ES) colonies exhibit a remarkable capacity to self-organize in vitro and recapitulate features associated with early embryogenesis.
source: Pioneering studies have suggested that both human and mouse embryonic stem cell (ES) colonies exhibit a remarkable capacity to self-organize in vitro and recapitulate features associated with early embryogenesis (Baillie-Johnson et al., 2015; Beccari et al., 2018; Doetschman et al., 1985; Shahbazi et al., 2019; Simunovic et al., 2019; Simunovic and Brivanlou, 2017; ten Berge et al., 2008; Turner et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2014; van den Brink et al., 2014; van den Brink et al., 2020; Warmflash et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites numerous previous studies on the self-organizing capacity of ES cell colonies.

claim: Homogeneous stimulation of human ES colonies cultured on 2-dimensional circular substrates with BMP4 ligands is sufficient to reproducibly generate radially symmetric colonies, where cells at the outmost rim differentiate into extraembryonic tissue, while the remaining cells differentiate progressively into more internal rings composed of the different embryonic germ layers.
source: For instance, homogeneous stimulation of human ES colonies cultured on 2-dimensional circular substrates with BMP4 ligands is sufficient to reproducibly generate radially symmetric colonies, where cells at the outmost rim differentiate into extraembryonic tissue, while the remaining cells differentiate progressively into more internal rings composed of the different embryonic germ layers - endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm (Warmflash et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the self-organizing capacity of human ES colonies.

claim: Apparent self-organizing processes in ES cell colonies are thought to rely on boundary sensing, community effects and the interplay between activators and inhibitors.
source: These apparent self-organizing processes are thought to rely on boundary sensing, community effects and the interplay between activators and inhibitors (Chhabra et al., 2019; Etoc et al., 2016; Nemashkalo et al., 2017; Sasai, 2013; Xavier da Silveira Dos Santos and Liberali, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the mechanisms underlying self-organization in ES cell colonies.

claim: Classical studies have established the dependency of embryonic development on both maternal factors and extraembryonic tissues.
source: While these pioneering studies suggest that embryonic tissues might have some self-organizing capacity, classical studies have also established the dependency of embryonic development on both maternal factors and extraembryonic tissues, thereby raising key questions as to their specific contributions to robust embryonic development.
evidence: The manuscript refers to classical studies on the role of maternal factors and extraembryonic tissues in embryonic development.
